con-b1-synthesize-client-documents-brief.q: You're building a kickoff briefing from three client documents. Why does the prompt require every claim to be tagged with its source?
options: It's the guardrail against hallucination and silent blending of facts across documents, the biggest risk when synthesizing multiple sources at once
It's a formatting requirement for uploading files to a Claude Project
It makes the briefing look more thorough
Tags are needed to sort the document alphabetically
con-b1-synthesize-client-documents-brief.why: Tagging each claim to its source is the direct guardrail against hallucination and silently blending facts from different documents into unflagged inferences.

con-b1-synthesize-client-documents-brief.q: The annual report and a prior consulting deck report different headcount figures for the same period. What should the briefing do?
options: Average the two figures together
Flag it explicitly as a contradiction rather than letting the AI silently pick one figure
Use whichever figure appears in the more recent-looking document
Omit headcount from the briefing entirely
con-b1-synthesize-client-documents-brief.why: The contradictions section exists to surface real inconsistencies explicitly, rather than letting the model quietly resolve them on its own.

con-b1-synthesize-client-documents-brief.q: Which of these is a mistake this lesson specifically warns against?
options: Uploading each document as a separate file into a Claude Project
Checking source-tagged claims against the original document
Pasting confidential materials into an account not covered by your firm's data-handling agreement
Asking for open questions to raise at the kickoff meeting
con-b1-synthesize-client-documents-brief.why: The lesson explicitly lists pasting confidential materials into an account outside your firm's data-handling agreement as a common mistake.

con-b2-structure-deliverable-storyline.q: Why does the prompt ask for 2-3 alternative storyline structures instead of one straight-to-outline draft?
options: Clients require multiple structures to be presented
It reduces the total number of findings needed
Alternative structures are faster to generate
It keeps structure a genuine choice you make, instead of accepting the model's first framing
con-b2-structure-deliverable-storyline.why: Asking for multiple options first keeps the consultant treating storyline structure as a real choice, rather than defaulting to the model's first framing.

con-b2-structure-deliverable-storyline.q: A finding doesn't fit cleanly into any proposed section. What should happen to it?
options: List it separately as 'doesn't fit — reconsider' rather than forcing it in or dropping it silently
Delete it from the findings list
Strengthen its wording so it fits the strongest section
Merge it into the closest-matching section regardless of fit
con-b2-structure-deliverable-storyline.why: The 'doesn't fit' list matters because forcing every finding into a tidy structure is how real deliverables end up misrepresenting or overreaching on evidence.

con-b2-structure-deliverable-storyline.q: The prompt explicitly bans which behavior?
options: Proposing more than one storyline structure
Inventing new findings or strengthening a finding's claim just to make it fit a section better
Writing a one-sentence 'so what' per section
Recommending a structure based on how well findings support it
con-b2-structure-deliverable-storyline.why: The explicit ban is against strengthening a finding's claim or inventing new findings just to make the storyline fit better, protecting evidence integrity.

con-i1-industry-research-before-proposal.q: Why does the lesson recommend reviewing and narrowing Gemini's proposed research plan before letting Deep Research run, rather than accepting a broad brief as-is?
options: Gemini charges extra for revising a research plan
Vague research briefs return fewer sources
It keeps the resulting report's sourcing traceable, rather than producing vague, uncited generalizations
Reviewing the plan is required by Gemini's interface before any run
con-i1-industry-research-before-proposal.why: Reviewing and narrowing the research brief before Deep Research runs keeps the report's sourcing traceable and reduces vague, uncited generalizations.

con-i1-industry-research-before-proposal.q: Before a statistic from a Gemini Deep Research report goes into a client-facing proposal, what must happen?
options: Nothing further — citations guarantee accuracy
Convert it into a percentage
Remove the citation to keep the proposal clean
Cross-check it against the primary source, not just Gemini's paraphrase
con-i1-industry-research-before-proposal.why: Even sourced answers can misread or overstate what a source says, so any statistic going into the proposal must be cross-checked against the primary source.

con-i1-industry-research-before-proposal.q: Which is a mistake this lesson specifically calls out?
options: Treating 'sourced' as automatically 'correct' and skipping independent verification of high-stakes claims
Prioritizing sources from the last 12 months
Giving Deep Research a specific, bounded research brief
Asking follow-up questions to narrow overly generic answers
con-i1-industry-research-before-proposal.why: The lesson warns against treating citations as proof of accuracy on their own, since even sourced answers need independent verification for high-stakes claims.

con-i2-slide-narratives-executive-summar.q: What's the key difference between a 'topic title' and an 'action title' for a consulting slide?
options: Action titles are always longer than 15 words
An action title states the conclusion the slide supports, not just a description of its topic
Topic titles are used only for appendix slides
Action titles require a chart, topic titles don't
con-i2-slide-narratives-executive-summar.why: An action title states a conclusion (what to do with the slide), while a topic title like 'Customer Retention Analysis' tells the reader nothing actionable.

con-i2-slide-narratives-executive-summar.q: A slide's data only shows correlation, but the drafted action title implies causation. What should happen?
options: Keep the title since it's more persuasive
Delete the underlying data from the slide
The AI should flag the slide so the consultant can revise the title or the content
Move the slide to the appendix
con-i2-slide-narratives-executive-summar.why: The prompt specifically asks the AI to flag any slide where the action title overstates what the underlying data actually shows, such as implying causation from correlation.

con-i2-slide-narratives-executive-summar.q: Why does the prompt ask for the action titles to also be listed alone, in sequence, at the end?
options: It's required for slide numbering
It replaces the need for an executive summary
It shortens the overall deck
It lets you read the whole deck's argument in about 30 seconds, close to how a rushed executive will actually experience it
con-i2-slide-narratives-executive-summar.why: Reading the standalone title list is close to how a rushed executive actually experiences the deck, so it's a fast check that the argument holds together.

con-i3-workshop-interview-preparation.q: Why does the prompt ask for a likely 'vague or deflective answer' and a follow-up probe for each core question?
options: It rehearses a probe in advance, closing the hesitation gap that happens when an interviewer gets a non-answer in real time
It's required for workshop facilitation software
It makes the interview guide longer
It replaces the need for warm-up questions
con-i3-workshop-interview-preparation.why: Pre-drafting the likely deflective answer and its follow-up probe improves real-time performance by closing the hesitation gap interviewers feel when they get a vague answer.

con-i3-workshop-interview-preparation.q: If the interview runs short on time, how should questions be cut according to the prompt?
options: Cut the warm-up questions only, keep everything else
Cut the questions least tied to the interview's core hypothesis first, keeping what's most load-bearing
Cut questions randomly to save time
Cut the closing open question only
con-i3-workshop-interview-preparation.why: The prompt ranks cuts by relevance to the hypothesis, protecting the interview's core purpose rather than losing the most important question to a tangent.

con-i3-workshop-interview-preparation.q: Which is a mistake this lesson specifically warns against?
options: Anchoring core questions to a specific hypothesis
Preparing a follow-up probe for vague answers
Using the same generic guide for every stakeholder regardless of role or likely candor
Requesting a facilitation structure for a group workshop
con-i3-workshop-interview-preparation.why: The lesson warns against reusing the same generic guide for every stakeholder, since role and likely candor should shape the questions.

con-a1-repeatable-engagement-workflow.q: Why must the 'Required Human Verification' column state a specific, checkable action instead of something like 'review carefully'?
options: Specific actions are required by consulting industry regulation
It makes the table shorter
Vague instructions take longer to write
A vague instruction means nothing to a new team member, while a specific action is checkable and actually enforces quality control
con-a1-repeatable-engagement-workflow.why: A specific, checkable action is usable as real quality control, while a vague instruction like 'review carefully' means nothing to a new team member.

con-a1-repeatable-engagement-workflow.q: The prompt instructs the AI not to invent a stage or task the consultant didn't describe. Why?
options: It keeps the workflow document honest about how the team actually currently works, rather than aspirational
Inventing stages would violate confidentiality rules
It reduces the number of tools needed
It's faster to generate a shorter document
con-a1-repeatable-engagement-workflow.why: Restricting the AI to only formalize described stages keeps the document honest about actual current practice instead of an aspirational, fuller-looking workflow.

con-a1-repeatable-engagement-workflow.q: How should the workflow document be validated before becoming the firm's standard reference?
options: Publish it immediately once the AI generates it
Review it against a real recent engagement and circulate it to a colleague to confirm it matches how the team actually works
Have only the person who wrote it review it
Skip review since the table format is self-explanatory
con-a1-repeatable-engagement-workflow.why: The lesson recommends reviewing the draft against a real engagement and having a colleague confirm it before adopting it as the standard reference.

pm-b1-meeting-notes-to-decisions-actions.q: An action item in your raw notes has no clearly stated owner. What should the structured summary do?
options: Assign it to whoever spoke most in the meeting
Assign it to the project manager by default
Write 'TBD' rather than guessing an owner
Omit the action item entirely
pm-b1-meeting-notes-to-decisions-actions.why: The instruction to write 'TBD' instead of guessing is the most important line in this prompt, preventing false accountability from an invented owner.

pm-b1-meeting-notes-to-decisions-actions.q: Why does the prompt separate 'decisions made' from 'open issues / parking lot' into different sections?
options: It's a formatting requirement of most PM tools
It makes the document longer
Decisions and open issues can't be discussed in the same meeting
It mirrors how project governance actually works — decisions are settled, open issues still need to come back on a future agenda
pm-b1-meeting-notes-to-decisions-actions.why: Splitting decisions from open issues mirrors real project governance: decisions are settled while open issues need to return to a future agenda.

pm-b1-meeting-notes-to-decisions-actions.q: Which is a mistake this lesson specifically warns against?
options: Letting the AI assign an owner or due date that wasn't actually agreed in the meeting
Sending the summary to attendees the same day
Reading the output against your raw notes before sending
Using consistent section headers every time
pm-b1-meeting-notes-to-decisions-actions.why: The lesson explicitly warns against letting the AI invent an owner or due date that wasn't actually agreed in the meeting.

pm-b2-status-reports-stakeholders-read.q: Who decides whether the project's overall status is 'on track,' 'at risk,' or 'off track' in this workflow?
options: The AI infers it from the rough notes provided
The PM decides and states it explicitly; the AI is told not to infer or change it based on the content
The stakeholder decides after reading the report
It's calculated automatically from the project timeline
pm-b2-status-reports-stakeholders-read.why: Requiring the PM to state the actual status prevents the amber-vs-green judgment call, which requires real project knowledge, from being outsourced to the AI.

pm-b2-status-reports-stakeholders-read.q: A report lists three active blockers but the status line says 'on track.' What does this violate?
options: The 200-word limit
The requirement to name what's needed from the reader
The instruction not to soften or exaggerate the stated status — the status line must honestly match the content
The instruction to use bullet points
pm-b2-status-reports-stakeholders-read.why: The prompt directly guards against a report reading more reassuring than the actual content warrants — the status line must match reality.

pm-b2-status-reports-stakeholders-read.q: Why does the prompt cap the report at under 200 words?
options: Email clients truncate longer reports
It's a hard technical limit of the AI tool
Shorter reports are required for legal reasons
It turns the report from a status dump into something a busy stakeholder can skim and act on in under a minute
pm-b2-status-reports-stakeholders-read.why: The strict word limit is what makes the report something a stakeholder can act on immediately, rather than a status dump nobody reads fully.

pm-i1-project-plans-work-breakdowns-from.q: Before generating the work breakdown structure, what does the prompt ask the AI to do first?
options: List the clarifying questions it would need answered to make the breakdown realistic, which the PM then answers
Generate three alternative breakdowns immediately
Estimate the total project budget
Ask the PM to choose a PM software tool
pm-i1-project-plans-work-breakdowns-from.why: Requiring clarifying questions before the plan itself keeps the output from being a generic template dressed up as your specific project.

pm-i1-project-plans-work-breakdowns-from.q: Why does the prompt require every task to be tagged as either '[from my input]' or '[typical pattern — verify]'?
options: It's a formatting requirement of most project tools
It stops a plausible-sounding but unverified task from being silently treated as fact, and lets the PM scan quickly for what needs judgment
It shortens the overall task list
Tags are needed to calculate the project budget
pm-i1-project-plans-work-breakdowns-from.why: Tagging every task by its source is the core guardrail against treating an unverified assumption as a confirmed fact in the plan.

pm-i1-project-plans-work-breakdowns-from.q: Which is a mistake this lesson specifically warns against?
options: Answering the clarifying questions before generating the plan
Treating the output as a first draft to correct
Accepting AI-estimated task durations without checking them against your team's actual historical velocity
Importing the corrected breakdown into your real PM tool
pm-i1-project-plans-work-breakdowns-from.why: The lesson warns against accepting AI-estimated durations without verifying them against your team's actual historical velocity and capacity.

pm-i2-risk-registers-mitigation-drafts.q: The AI drafts a mitigation that just says 'monitor closely.' What does the lesson say about this?
options: It's an acceptable default for low-impact risks
It should be used for every risk to save time
It's the correct mitigation for high-likelihood risks
It's too vague to be useful — a mitigation should state a concrete action and, where relevant, a trigger for when to act
pm-i2-risk-registers-mitigation-drafts.why: Vague phrases like 'monitor closely' are exactly what the prompt requires the AI to avoid, in favor of a concrete action and trigger for when to act.

pm-i2-risk-registers-mitigation-drafts.q: Why are AI-suggested additional risk categories kept in a separate 'risks to consider adding' section instead of merged into the main register?
options: Only the PM knows which risks genuinely apply to this specific project, so suggestions shouldn't be treated as confirmed without review
Merging them would exceed the table's column limit
The main register can only contain risks with assigned owners
Separate sections are required by most risk-management software
pm-i2-risk-registers-mitigation-drafts.why: Keeping AI-suggested risks separate respects that only the PM can confirm which risks genuinely apply, rather than treating suggestions as automatically valid.

pm-i2-risk-registers-mitigation-drafts.q: Which is a mistake this lesson specifically warns against?
options: Leaving the owner field blank in the initial AI draft
Building the register once at kickoff and never revisiting it as the project's real risk profile changes
Rating risks only based on what was stated in the project summary
Proposing additional risk categories separately from the main list
pm-i2-risk-registers-mitigation-drafts.why: The lesson warns that a register built once at kickoff and never revisited loses credibility and misses the project's evolving actual risk profile.

pm-i3-stakeholder-communications-difficu.q: The prompt instructs the AI to lead the message with the fact, not an apology or a long buildup. Why?
options: It's shorter to write that way
Apologies are considered unprofessional in all business writing
Burying bad news under preamble reads as evasive and makes the reader search for the actual point
It matches most corporate style guides
pm-i3-stakeholder-communications-difficu.why: Leading with the fact rather than an apology is a deliberate structural choice, since burying bad news reads as evasive and forces the reader to hunt for the point.

pm-i3-stakeholder-communications-difficu.q: What is the critical guardrail regarding dates and commitments in this prompt?
options: The AI must always include a specific recovery date
Dates should be omitted from all difficult messages
The AI should ask the reader to propose a new date
The AI must not add a new promised date or outcome the PM hasn't actually confirmed
pm-i3-stakeholder-communications-difficu.why: This is the critical guardrail: an AI trying to sound reassuring might invent a recovery date the PM never confirmed, turning an honest update into a broken promise.

pm-i3-stakeholder-communications-difficu.q: Which is a mistake this lesson specifically warns against?
options: Using corporate hedging language that technically communicates nothing concrete
Ending the message with a single clear ask
Stating the reason for the issue briefly and factually
Keeping the message under 150 words
pm-i3-stakeholder-communications-difficu.why: Corporate hedging phrases are directly targeted by the lesson because they dilute a difficult message into vague language that says nothing concrete.

pm-a1-pm-operating-system-templates-work.q: One of your five recurring tasks (the risk register) doesn't have a defined verification step in your notes. What should the AI do?
options: Invent a plausible verification step so the table looks complete
Flag it under a 'needs a defined verification step' note rather than inventing one for the PM
Leave that row out of the table entirely
Copy the verification step from a different task
pm-a1-pm-operating-system-templates-work.why: Flagging missing verification steps instead of inventing one protects the integrity of the whole system — a made-up step would give false confidence.

pm-a1-pm-operating-system-templates-work.q: Why does the operating-system table include 'Cadence' and 'Output Destination' columns, not just the task and tool?
options: Those columns are required by most spreadsheet templates
They replace the need for a verification column
A PM under deadline pressure needs to know at a glance which template to reach for and where the result goes
They're only relevant for weekly tasks
pm-a1-pm-operating-system-templates-work.why: Cadence and destination columns are what make the table usable day-to-day, letting a PM under pressure know at a glance which template applies and where output goes.

pm-a1-pm-operating-system-templates-work.q: Before treating the assembled operating system as final, what does the lesson recommend?
options: Publish it immediately since the AI already validated it
Have only the PM who wrote it review it once
Skip testing since the individual prompts were already proven
Test it on a real live project for one full cycle, such as one sprint or reporting period
pm-a1-pm-operating-system-templates-work.why: Testing the assembled system on one real full cycle catches gaps that only show up under real project conditions, before it's treated as final.
